topStories.headline: Police Chase Ends in Multi-Vehicle Crash at S. Van Ness and 14th, Nine Hurt
topStories.dek: A Sunday-night pursuit through the Mission District left two people critically injured and reignited debate over SFPD's high-speed chase policy.
topStories.body:
A police pursuit through the heart of the Mission District ended in a violent multi-vehicle collision on Sunday, July 20, sending nine people to the hospital and flooding the intersection of South Van Ness Avenue and 14th Street after a fire hydrant was sheared from its foundation.

San Francisco Police Department officers first spotted a pickup truck driving erratically near Guerrero and 19th streets. When officers attempted a traffic stop, the vehicle fled. The truck eventually slammed into a second, occupied car at South Van Ness and 14th Street — directly outside the Audi dealership at 300 South Van Ness — causing the struck vehicle to strike the hydrant and damage the dealership's glass storefront.

San Francisco Fire Department crews treated nine people at the scene. Two occupants of the fleeing vehicle were transported with critical injuries; six others sustained minor to moderate injuries; and one additional person was evaluated but declined hospital transport. Officers detained the driver and four other occupants of the suspect vehicle, whose ages ranged from 13 to 24. Charges remain pending.

The crash touched off a fresh round of community criticism of the SFPD's pursuit policy. Under SFPD policy 5.05, officers are required to weigh the urgency of apprehending a suspect against the danger a chase creates for the public and are directed to call off pursuits when that danger becomes unreasonable. South Van Ness Avenue is part of the city's designated "high-injury network" — a stretch of roadway with a documented history of serious crashes. The intersection remained closed well into Monday morning while cleanup crews dealt with vehicular wreckage and localized flooding from the compromised water main. The investigation is ongoing, and SFPD has not released additional details about what prompted the initial traffic stop.

topStories.headline: 'The Great Drain Robber': Mystery Thief Keeps Stealing Bernal Heights Sewer Grates
topStories.dek: A slow-moving crime wave that began in April has puzzled residents, stumped police, and left homeowners on the hook for costly sidewalk repairs.
topStories.body:
For months, a mystery figure has been prowling Bernal Heights in the early hours of the morning — not to steal bikes or catalytic converters, but sewer vent grates. The small, square metal covers are designed to keep debris from clogging sewer system air vents and dot sidewalks throughout the neighborhood, yet someone keeps prying them loose and carting them away.

Security cameras on Mullen Avenue, Brewster Street, Montcalm Street, and Macedonia Avenue have all captured the same routine: a tall, slim man arrives around 3 a.m. wearing a headlamp, clears leaves from around the grate, frees it with a screwdriver, slips it into a grocery cart, and moves on to the next target. The whole operation takes less than a minute. On one street, the same grate had been stolen and replaced three times since April.

What baffles neighbors most is the economics. Scrap metal dealers report the mixed-steel grates yield only about three to five cents per pound — meaning roughly 32 grates to earn a dollar. Yet the costs fall squarely on homeowners: under Section 706 of the San Francisco Public Works Code, property owners are responsible for maintaining their adjacent sidewalks, including missing sewer vent covers. San Francisco Public Works has been issuing 30-day repair notices to affected residents, with replacement costs estimated by the city at around $40 per unit — though some residents have found replacements for as little as $10.

The San Francisco Police Department has acknowledged receiving reports but stated it has not identified a broader trend or made any arrests. Residents have dubbed the perpetrator 'the Great Drain Robber' and say they have taken to checking their sidewalks every morning. Some have improvised solutions — placing upside-down traffic cones over holes or weighting down plastic lids with rocks — to warn pedestrians. Mission Local first reported the story, which was later picked up by NBC Bay Area and ABC7.

topStories.headline: Bernal Heights Playground Reopens After $1.3 Million Renovation — and Becomes a City First
topStories.dek: The newly rebuilt playground at 500 Moultrie Street is the inaugural project under San Francisco's streamlined Playground Renewal Program, cutting delivery time from years to months.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Recreation and Park Department celebrated the reopening of the Bernal Heights Playground in late 2025, unveiling a $1.3 million redesign that replaced outdated play structures with modern, fully accessible equipment and set a new standard for how the city delivers park improvements. The playground at 500 Moultrie Street is now open and welcoming families after construction that began in August 2025 and was completed in record time.

Bernal Heights Playground is the first project completed under San Francisco's new Playground Renewal Program, which uses a cooperative purchasing contracting method to dramatically speed up playground delivery and reduce costs. The approach — made possible through legislation approved by the Board of Supervisors — allows Rec and Park to purchase and install high-quality play equipment through pre-bid contracts shared by multiple agencies, cutting out layers of red tape and reducing contractor markups. The new framework shortens timelines from what previously took several years to just 12–18 months.

Guided by community input gathered through design surveys and in-person feedback sessions, the renovation features new play structures made from durable Robinia wood, a large slide, monkey bars, climbing elements, improved grading and drainage, and new accessible surfacing to ensure children of all abilities can use the space. Recreation and Park General Manager Phil Ginsburg said the improvements ensure that 'every child, regardless of ability, can safely play, explore, and create memories in a welcoming space.'

District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder, whose district includes Bernal Heights, called the renovation 'a much needed improvement for the community.' The playground has long served as a gathering point for neighborhood families and is already drawing new visitors since reopening.

moreNews.headline: Former KFC/Taco Bell Site to Become Mission Music Studio for Independent Artists
moreNews.body: A long-shuttered fast-food building in the Mission District is slated to be transformed into a music studio designed to support independent and emerging local musicians and artists. CBS San Francisco first reported the conversion, which community advocates see as a creative reuse of a neglected commercial space. Details on the operator and opening timeline have not yet been publicly released.

moreNews.headline: SF Lowrider Parade Airs on Live Television for the First Time
moreNews.body: San Francisco's annual Lowrider Parade, a decades-long tradition in the Mission District, was broadcast on live television for the first time this summer, bringing wider attention to a cultural institution rooted in the neighborhood's Latino heritage. Community leader Roberto Hernandez, sometimes called the 'Mayor of the Mission,' has long championed lowrider culture as a symbol of pride and resilience. The parade's television debut marks a milestone in the movement's broader recognition.

moreNews.headline: Puddle Jumpers Co-op Daycare Closes Its Doors in the Mission
moreNews.body: Puddle Jumpers, one of the Mission District's rare parent-run cooperative daycares, has closed after years of operation, according to Mission Local. The closure ends a chapter for one of the neighborhood's distinctive community-run childcare institutions, reflecting broader pressures on small nonprofits and cooperative organizations across San Francisco.
